chapter: Early string bands and first jobs
title: Bat Steckler and changing keys on cornet
summary: Asked how he got started, Mello recalls hearing Bat Steckler, who could play in any key by swapping crooks, and rehearsals he attended.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Yeah, I'm gonna get a cigarette. Uh, I was wondering something. How did you get your start in music?
Did you hear any other music than your father playing the harmonica?

I heard Brad Stecker, the oldest trumpet player in the city right now. He was, uh, he used to play with, uh, I used to do a little reporting for the International Jazz. That's a year, four years back. And, uh, they used to rehearse once a week on a Wednesday night. On. With a good Betholome in there. Dolphine. And I used to go there. Well, my daddy was a pretty good friend of Shanks. And, uh, I used to go over there and listen to him. Now, I'll say this for Bat Steckler. He could do what I couldn't do. Bat Steckler could take a horn and put a horn in C, in sharps. And play in flats. Or he could put a horn in flats and play in sharps. That's what he could do. That same Bat Steckler you wanted to see. Do you mean by changing the slides? No, he'd never change the flats and things. He never had no slides. And he only had, he used to have two crooks. He had an A crook and a B crook. Little bit of crooks. But one of the B was about that B flat. And the A was about that long. But when he put the A on, it threw his horn in the sharps. He was a C then. Well, he never did do that. If he had that C crook on, well, he just up it on. That's all in play. And he didn't do that. And he didn't do that. So, I tell him that many times. I said Bat got a dog and I said you can do something that I couldn't do. And I tried it time and again. He said, all right, try and put your horn in B flat. And then, try to play in C or in D or in G or you're gonna fight. So, oh, he says, you used to get the tone out of the horn. Yeah, I said, but I couldn't get the difference. I said, no, they had three valves to work. I said, how'd you do it? Well, he said, we did it. I know he did because Johnny Gormason, Johnny Shank used to play practically all in C. But, sometime, he'd get a piece of playing F on B flat. But, I never had changed no crook. No, no, uh-uh. No. And I've seen that. I can still see the four of them sitting there. And that's over 60 years ago.
